bibliography.abstract: As global population ageing accelerates, urban environments face increasing pressure to address the complex and evolving needs of older adults. While prior research on urban design for older people (UDFOP) has largely concentrated on spatial accessibility and service provision, systematic insights into the field's thematic evolution and future direction remain limited. This study adopts a hybrid analytical approach—integrating S-curve life-cycle modelling, Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), and cosine similarity calculations—to examine 787 publications from 2016 to 2025. By segmenting the timeline into four development stages, the study reveals: (a) a structured thematic shift from community planning and participation (2016–2019), to transport accessibility and health risk (2020–2021), and design solutions and ageing needs (2022–2023), culminating in smart and inclusive ageing strategies (2024–2025); (b) three evolutionary roadmaps: healthy ageing and smart environment, neighbourhood and spatial equity, and policy and service provision; (c) increasing focus on neighbourhood-scale spatial analysis and lived experience; (d) growing integration of walkability, green infrastructure, and perceived quality of life; (e) emerging adoption of computational methods—including GIS, machine learning, and spatial analytics—in response to urban challenges; and (f) a novel three-dimensional conceptual framework linking demographic patterns, spatial form and governance mechanisms. This study contributes theoretically by uncovering UDFOP's developmental logic and transition structure; methodologically by demonstrating the utility of hybrid computational approaches in tracking thematic evolution; and practically by offering an evidence-based framework for inclusive, equitable, and technology-integrated age-friendly urban strategies, with implications for planners, policymakers, and researchers.

en.caveats: The analysis is restricted to the thematic trends present within the selected academic literature database and does not evaluate the real-world implementation or efficacy of these urban design strategies.
en.what: This study maps the thematic evolution of urban design for older people by analyzing 787 publications spanning 2016 to 2025. Using a hybrid analytical approach that combines S-curve life-cycle modeling, Latent Dirichlet Allocation topic modeling, and cosine similarity, the researchers traced the field's progression across four distinct stages and identified three primary evolutionary roadmaps: healthy ageing and smart environments, neighborhood and spatial equity, and policy and service provision.
en.why: It establishes a structured, computational framework that tracks how research has shifted from basic community planning toward smart, inclusive, and technology-integrated urban strategies, providing planners with an evidence-based roadmap of emerging design priorities.
